Main article: [Twitter trends](/wiki/Twitter_trends "Twitter trends")

Twitter introduced its "trends" feature in mid-2008, an algorithmic lists of trending topics among users.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144) A word or phrase mentioned can become "trending topic" based on an algorithm.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144) Because a relatively small number of users can affect trending topics through a concerted campaign, the feature has been the targeted of concerted manipulation campaigns.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144) While some campaigns are innocuous, others have promoted conspiracy theories or hoaxes, or sought to amplify extremist messages.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144) Some featured trends are globally displayed, while others are limited to a specific country.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144)

A 2021 study by [EPFL](/wiki/%C3%89cole_Polytechnique_F%C3%A9d%C3%A9rale_de_Lausanne "École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne") researchers found that frequent "ephemeral [astroturfing](/wiki/Astroturfing "Astroturfing")" efforts targeted at Trends; from 2015 to 2019, "47% of local trends in Turkey and 20% of global trends are fake, created from scratch by bots...The fake trends discovered include [phishing](/wiki/Phishing "Phishing") apps, gambling promotions, disinformation campaigns, political slogans, [hate speech](/wiki/Hate_speech "Hate speech") against vulnerable populations and even marriage proposals."[[142]](#cite_note-145)[[143]](#cite_note-146) The *[MIT Technology Review](/wiki/MIT_Technology_Review "MIT Technology Review")* reported that, as of 2022, Twitter "sometimes manually overrides particularly objectionable trends" and, for some trends, used both algorithmic and human input to select representative tweets with context.[[141]](#cite_note-Ohlheiser2022-144)

In 2007, cancer was the number one cause of death, contributing to 29.6% of all deaths in Canada. The second highest cause of death was cardiovascular diseases, resulting in 21.5% of deaths. In 2011, prostate cancer was the most common form of cancer among males (about 28% of all new cases) and breast cancer the most common in females (also about 28% of all new cases).

The leading cause of death in both males and females is lung cancer, which contributes to 26.8% of all cancer deaths. Statistics indicate that between the ages of 20 and 50 years, the incidence rate of cancer is higher amongst women whereas after 50 years of age, the incidence rate increases in men. Predictions by the Canadian Cancer Society indicate that with time, there will be an increase in the rates of incidence of cancer for both males and females.

The team joined the [Central League](/wiki/Central_League "Central League") in December 1949 as the **Hiroshima Carp**. They were named the Carp after the [koi fish](/wiki/Koi "Koi") that climbed the rapids of [Hiroshima Castle](/wiki/Hiroshima_Castle "Hiroshima Castle"), chosen to signify Hiroshima's rebirth and perseverance following the aforementioned atomic bombings. Said name was put forth by a politician named Noboru Tanigawa, who was the face of Hiroshima's bid. Another name put forward was Greens, after a successful semi-professional team of the same name. Others included Bears, Rainbows, Doves, and morbidly, Atoms. However, all the names were put aside, as Tanigawa was so influential to the team's bid, he always had the final decision.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The alliance, however, collapsed in the 1490s; the invasion of [Charles VIII of France](/wiki/Charles_VIII_of_France "Charles VIII of France") initiated a series of wars in the peninsula. In the middle of such conflicts, the Medici popes [Leo X](/wiki/Leo_X "Leo X") (1513–1521) and [Clement VII](/wiki/Clement_VII "Clement VII") (1523–1534) faced the [Protestant Reformation](/wiki/Protestant_Reformation "Protestant Reformation") in Germany, England and elsewhere.

In the [1964–65 season](/wiki/1964%E2%80%9365_NBA_season "1964–65 NBA season"), the 76ers acquired from the Warriors [Wilt Chamberlain](/wiki/Wilt_Chamberlain "Wilt Chamberlain"), a high school legend at Philadelphia's Overbrook High School who had begun his career with the Warriors in the city. The 76ers pushed the Celtics to seven games in the semifinals, with the 76ers trailing 110–109 in Game 7. After [Hal Greer](/wiki/Hal_Greer "Hal Greer")'s pass was stolen by [John Havlicek](/wiki/John_Havlicek "John Havlicek"), the Celtics beat the [Los Angeles Lakers](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") and won the NBA Championship.
